frames.narration: A customer wants to import a file of 2,000,000 rows, about 600 MB. The app asks the API for an upload, with an idempotency key. The API creates an upload session and a job, and tells the app to send 75 chunks of 8 MB.
The app sends chunks straight into storage, each with its number. After 41 chunks (numbers 0 to 40) the phone loses its network, and the upload stops half way.
The network returns. The app asks what the server has, and learns that chunks 0 to 40 are safe. It sends only the missing 34 chunks, so nothing is uploaded twice. 41 plus 34 is 75.

The app says the upload is complete. The API checks that all 75 chunks are present, marks the job as queued, and puts it on the queue. It answers at once with the job id, so the app does not wait for the import.

A fair scheduler hands the worker one chunk at a time, taking turns between tenants, so this big job does not block small ones. The worker reads the chunk from storage and checks every row as it goes, without loading the whole file.

Valid rows are written to the database in batches of 1,000, as upserts by their key, so a repeated batch changes nothing. Bad rows are not written: they go into an error report with their line number and the reason.

The job finishes: 1,999,412 rows written and 588 rejected, which makes 2,000,000. The error report is saved next to the file, and the job moves to done with errors. An app that polls the job sees the same.
The webhook sender calls the customer's endpoint with a signed message, so the app does not have to poll. If the endpoint is down, the sender retries with growing delays.
The app times out and sends the create request again with the same key k-55. The API finds the existing job and returns job-12, so there is no second import and no duplicate rows.
Later the customer asks to export the same data. A worker reads from the database in pages and writes compressed parts of the file into storage, and the job table shows how far it has got.

When the file is ready the customer gets a link signed by the server that works for 15 minutes. They download straight from storage, so the API does not carry the bytes. After 15 minutes the same link is refused.
